papers.title: SpaAxFormer: Fine-Grained Token Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Axial Transformers
papers.summary: SpaAxFormer is a deep learning model that applies axial transformer architectures to analyze spatial transcriptomics data at a fine-grained, token-level resolution. It aims to better capture spatial gene expression patterns by breaking down the analysis into row-wise and column-wise attention mechanisms, improving computational efficiency while preserving spatial context. This approach could enhance the detection of localized gene expression signatures across tissue sections compared to standard transformer models.
papers.why: This method could improve spatial transcriptomics analysis of brain tissue, potentially enabling more precise mapping of gene expression patterns in interneurons and perineuronal net-associated regions relevant to mitophagy and autophagy studies.
papers.figure: Figure showing the axial attention mechanism applied to spatial transcriptomics data, likely depicting token-level spatial gene expression maps and model architecture.

papers.title: Role of Cdk5 in Mitochondrial Dysfunction: Phosphorylation of KANSL1 and Impairment of PINK1-Mediated Mitophagy
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the kinase Cdk5 contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction in neurons. It finds that Cdk5 phosphorylates KANSL1, a protein involved in chromatin regulation, and this modification disrupts PINK1-mediated mitophagy, the process that normally clears damaged mitochondria. The result is impaired mitochondrial quality control, which may contribute to neuronal stress or degeneration.
papers.why: Understanding how Cdk5-driven phosphorylation events disrupt PINK1-mediated mitophagy provides direct mechanistic insight relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.

papers.title: Synergistic regulation of neuroinflammation by mitophagy and the cGAS-STING pathway following ischemic stroke.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, interacts with the cGAS-STING innate immune pathway to regulate inflammation after ischemic stroke. Damaged mitochondria release DNA that can trigger cGAS-STING signaling, promoting neuroinflammation, while effective mitophagy can limit this activation. The abstract suggests a synergistic relationship where these two pathways jointly shape the inflammatory response and potentially neuronal outcomes after stroke.
papers.why: Understanding how mitophagy regulates mitochondrial DNA release and innate immune activation in neurons provides mechanistic insight relevant to your work on mitophagy's role in neuronal stress responses, even though this paper focuses on stroke rather than spatial omics or interneurons specifically.

papers.title: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy
papers.summary: This study used high-content screening to test many FDA-approved drugs for their ability to activate mitophagy, the process by which cells clear damaged mitochondria. The researchers likely used fluorescent reporter assays in cells to identify compounds that boost mitophagy signals. The result is a list of existing, clinically approved drugs that could be repurposed as mitophagy activators for further study or therapeutic use.
papers.why: Identifying FDA-approved mitophagy activators could provide ready-to-use pharmacological tools to manipulate mitophagy in neurons, directly supporting the project's focus on mitophagy mechanisms and potentially enabling intervention studies paired with spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics readouts in brain tissue.

papers.title: Activation of AMPK/mTOR-Mediated Autophagy by Tanshinone IIA Facilitates Neural Repair after Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how Tanshinone IIA, a compound derived from a traditional Chinese medicinal herb, affects spinal cord injury recovery. The researchers found that this compound activates autophagy (the cell's internal cleanup process) through the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway. This activation appears to promote neural repair and improve outcomes after spinal cord injury.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates AMPK/mTOR-mediated autophagy regulation in neural tissue, which is directly applicable to mechanisms of mitophagy and autophagy being studied in neurons within the brain.

papers.title: Platelet lysates ameliorate impaired neuronal autophagy in Parkinson's Disease: correlative evidence for ROS/Akt signaling.
papers.summary: This study investigates whether platelet lysates can restore normal autophagy function in neurons affected by Parkinson's Disease. The researchers find correlative evidence linking this improvement to changes in ROS (reactive oxygen species) and Akt signaling pathways. The work suggests platelet-derived factors may represent a therapeutic avenue for addressing autophagy dysfunction in neurodegeneration.
papers.why: This paper is relevant to the profile's focus on neuronal autophagy dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease, offering mechanistic insight into signaling pathways (ROS/Akt) that could inform mitophagy-related investigations in the brain.

papers.title: AMPK/PINK1/Parkin pathway-associated mitochondrial quality control contributes to magnesium sulfate-induced neuroprotection in postoperative cognitive dysfunction
papers.summary: This study investigates how magnesium sulfate protects the brain against postoperative cognitive dysfunction, a common complication after surgery. The researchers found that magnesium sulfate activates a cellular energy-sensing pathway (AMPK) that connects to PINK1/Parkin, a key mitochondrial quality control system responsible for clearing damaged mitochondria through mitophagy. This improved mitochondrial health in neurons appears to underlie the cognitive protection observed, suggesting a therapeutic mechanism involving mitochondrial maintenance in the brain.
papers.why: This paper directly examines the AMPK/PINK1/Parkin mitophagy pathway in neurons, a core mechanistic focus of the PhD project, offering insight into pharmacological modulation of mitochondrial quality control that could inform spatial studies of neuronal stress responses.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in Parkinson's disease and aging
papers.summary: This paper reviews evidence that mitochondrial dysfunction is a central driver of neuronal loss in Parkinson's disease and in normal brain aging. It covers mechanisms such as impaired oxidative phosphorylation, increased reactive oxygen species, and defective mitochondrial quality control that contribute to dopaminergic neuron vulnerability. It likely discusses how aging exacerbates these mitochondrial defects, creating a cumulative burden that predisposes neurons to degeneration.
papers.why: Understanding mitochondrial dysfunction mechanisms in PD and aging provides essential background for studying mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, which is central to this PhD project.
